source.source_summary: Fully original relationship drama about a woman learning through her best friend that her boyfriend has an active dating profile and is messaging new matches while sitting across from her.

selected.title: His Dating Profile Said He Was Newly Single
selected.hook: My boyfriend's dating profile said he was newly single. We had dinner plans that night.
selected.voiceover:
My boyfriend's dating profile said he was ‘newly single.’ We had dinner plans that night.

My best friend sent me the screenshot at 4:12 p.m. She'd reopened a dating app after a breakup, and his profile appeared three swipes in.

Same photos. Same job. Same neighborhood. One detail was new: ‘Looking for something spontaneous.’

When he arrived for dinner, I didn't mention it. I asked how his day was. He said boring. Then his phone lit up with a notification from the exact app.

He froze.

His first explanation was that the account was old. I showed him the screenshot. It said ‘active today.’

Then he claimed his friends had reactivated it as a prank.

So I asked him to open the messages.

He refused, saying that would reward my lack of trust.

That almost worked until my best friend sent another screenshot. Before telling me anything, she'd matched with him using a profile he didn't recognize.

He had messaged her first.

Not months ago. Twenty-three minutes earlier.

And the message wasn't subtle: ‘You free tonight?’

He was sitting across from me when he sent it.

I paid for my half, stood up, and told him he was finally telling the truth about one thing on his profile: he was newly single.

Now he's telling our friends I ended three years over ‘one stupid message.’

Would you call that one message, or proof of the plan behind it?
selected.youtube_description:
A best friend's dating-app screenshot turns an ordinary dinner into a live test of trust. Her boyfriend insists the profile is old, then blames a prank—but the timestamps tell a different story. This relationship drama about dating apps, cheating boundaries, and digital receipts asks a simple question: can one message prove an entire plan?
